title: The bodhisattva
hookLine: one who seeks awakening for the sake of all beings

cards: A splinter in your foot. Nobody has to call a meeting about it. Your hand doesn't stop to ask whether the foot deserves help, or whether this is really the hand's problem.
It just reaches down and pulls the thing out.

A Buddhist poet named Shantideva leaned on that same plain fact, the hand looking after the foot, to explain the figure at the heart of the great vehicle: the one who sets out to wake up, not for themselves alone, but for everyone.

teach.b: First, the word. Bodhisattva. Bodhi is awakening.
Sattva is usually explained as a being. An awakening being, or a being set on awakening.

This path met the word long ago in the Jataka tales, where it names the Buddha in his earlier lives, and Theravada Buddhists honor that path too. In the great vehicle, it becomes a path many are invited to walk.

teach.h: THE MIND OF AWAKENING TURNS OUTWARD.
teach.b: Mahayana teachers speak of bodhicitta, the mind of awakening, which you met on day three hundred twelve: the moment a person's wish for freedom turns outward and includes everyone.
Shantideva's long poem, The Way of the Bodhisattva, is largely about that turn: how to give rise to that mind, guard it, and keep it from going out. Third, the body.
In the poem Shantideva asks, in paraphrase: why protect one person's pain and not another's? The hand protects the foot because they're one body.
Many limbs, one body. So too, he says, with beings. Their suffering isn't someone else's business any more than your foot is someone else's foot.
He even practices trading places in his imagination, putting himself where another person stands, and looking back. Fourth, how it's lived.
In Mahayana communities, people recite vows to free all beings, and the vow is not meant to be finished by Friday. It's a direction more than a task.
For the sake of all can look like large things. It can also look like a hand reaching down for a foot, quickly, without a meeting.

how: In Mahayana communities, practitioners recite bodhisattva vows to free all beings, and Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva is studied in Tibetan traditions as a guide to giving rise to bodhicitta.

o: a being set on awakening for the sake of all
a monk who has finished the path and left
a teacher who founds a new Buddhist school

games.q: for the sake of all: tap the pairs.
p: the mind of awakening, turned outward

s: the word bodhisattva appears only in Mahayana texts
this path met it in the Jataka tales, naming the Buddha in his earlier lives.
Shantideva compares beings to the limbs of one body
the hand protects the foot because they're one body. so too with beings.
the bodhisattva vow is a task meant to be finished quickly
it's a direction more than a task, lived out in small acts.

games.q: you're the hand, and there's a splinter in the foot. what do you do?
o: ask whether the foot deserves help
reach down and pull it out
leave it: it's the foot's problem
games.why: Shantideva's point: the hand doesn't ask. many limbs, one body. the bodhisattva treats others' pain the same way.

practice: Feel your hands resting and your feet on the floor, and notice how they belong to one body.
Then let the circle grow, to the people in your home, on your street, people you'll never meet, and ask quietly what one small thing could help, even a little, beyond yourself.
Wait for an answer that's simple and real, and hold it.

wordCard.voice: Bodhisattva. A being set on awakening, not for themselves alone, but for the sake of all beings. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bodhi, awakening, and sattva, usually explained as a being. the Pali form is bodhisatta.

carryVoice: Your line: for the sake of all. Many limbs, one body, and a hand that just reaches. That's today, done.
